The Remainder of Chapter One: The Analysis of Form (Rūpa-vibhaṅga). Question:
"I have already understood those derived forms that are comprised within the sense organs (*indriya*).
Now I wish to hear about those not comprised within the sense organs; please explain their characteristics.
Answer:
Regarding the unmanifest [form] associated with visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles: herein, "visible form" refers to excellent manifest colors and so forth.
If blue, yellow, and other such colors do not undergo transformation or decay, they are called excellent manifest colors;
if they do undergo transformation or decay, they are called inferior manifest colors.
That which is neutral is called the "form resembling a location" (*pratibhāsa-sthāna-rūpa*) between the two.
Question:
There are two types of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*):
First, color; second, shape.
Why is it that only color (varṇa) is discussed here?
Answer:
Now, within this context, one should state as follows:

Form is of two kinds—the first being color (varṇa) and the second being shape (saṃsthāna). Color refers to blue, yellow, and so forth; shape refers to long, short, and so forth. What is the intention behind not mentioning [these]?

This means that visible forms (*rūpa*) are coarse and easily known. Thus, these various forms are cognized by two consciousnesses among the six: namely, the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

First, the eye-consciousness apprehends only their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); subsequently, the mental consciousness apprehends both their specific and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). That is to say, when those various forms abide in the present, the eye-consciousness can only apprehend their specific characteristics; immediately following the eye-consciousness, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises to again apprehend the specific or general characteristics of the previously perceived forms.

However, this subsequently arising conceptual mental consciousness (manovijñāna) relies upon the preceding visual consciousness and takes the preceding visible object as its condition; thus, when this mental consciousness is actually present, both its support and its object exist in the past.

Because these five objects, while abiding in the present, cannot have their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) discerned by the mental consciousness, the objective sphere of form is cognized by two types of consciousness: namely, when visual consciousness is present, it discerns only the present specific characteristic, which is not common [to other times].

When the various mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) manifest, they comprehend both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the three periods of time, because the objects of mental consciousness are universal and possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Immediately following visual consciousness, mental consciousness does not necessarily arise; rather, any one of the six classes of consciousness may arise accordingly.

If mental consciousness were to arise determinately immediately after visual consciousness, then the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) could not serve as the immediate antecedent condition for suffering and the other faculties, because the faculty of suffering exists only within the five bodies of sensory consciousness.
If that were so, it would contradict what is stated in the *Indriya-skandha*. As it says:

"The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) acts as the cause, the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya), and the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) for the faculty of suffering. However, this statement was made because, after the visual consciousness has cognized a form, it immediately gives rise to a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*vikalpaka-manovijñāna*). Thus, it was said.
Visual consciousness cognizes first; once visual consciousness has experienced [the object], mental consciousness subsequently cognizes it.

There are two kinds of sounds, and so forth, as explained at length: those consisting of appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which refers to those primary elements that, in their present moment, are included within the category of sentient beings.

"Non-appropriated primary elements" refers to those primary elements that are categorized as belonging to sentient beings in the past or future, as well as those categorized as not belonging to sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Among these, sound produced from appropriated primary elements is called "having appropriated primary elements as its cause."
This is because the appropriated great elements (mahābhūta) serve as five kinds of causes—such as the previously arisen cause—for the sound produced by them;
the same applies to sound that has non-appropriated great elements as its cause.
If sound arises from the mouth, the hands, or other such [parts of the body], it is called sound caused by appropriated great elements (*upātta-mahābhūta-hetuka-śabda*).
If it arises from forests, water, wind, and so forth, it is called sound caused by non-appropriated great elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta-hetuka-śabda*).
The rest is as explained previously.

Regarding all odors, and so forth in detail: those that are pleasing are called "good odors," those that are unpleasing are called "bad odors," and those that accord with the state of equanimity are called "neutral odors."
That which is smelled by the nose is the objective sphere of the nose-faculty; the rest is as explained previously.

Regarding all tastes, and so forth in detail: those that are pleasing are called "tastes of the agreeable," those that are not pleasing are called "tastes of the disagreeable," and those that differ from both are called "tastes of the domain of equanimity."
That which is tasted by the tongue is called the objective sphere of the tongue-faculty; the rest is as explained previously.
Question:
When tasting a flavor, does the tongue-consciousness arise first, or does the body-consciousness arise first?
Answer:

If cold, heat, and so forth predominate, then body-consciousness arises first; if saltiness, acidity, and so forth predominate, then tongue-consciousness arises first; even when touch and taste are equal, tongue-consciousness still arises first because the desire for taste is superior.

"A portion of the tangible," and so forth, as explained at length: "smoothness" refers to softness; "roughness" refers to coarseness and hardness; "lightness" refers to that which cannot be weighed; "heaviness" refers to that which can be weighed; "cold" refers to the arising of a desire for warmth when one is pressed by it; "hunger" refers to the desire for food; and "thirst" refers to the desire for drink.
These seven kinds are subsumed under the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), having derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) as their intrinsic nature.

Although the preceding four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are also subsumed under the sense-base of tangibles, they do not have derived matter as their intrinsic nature; therefore, there are eleven kinds within the sense-base of tangibles, of which these seven are derived and are thus called "a portion."
That which is touched by the body refers to the object of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*); the rest is as explained previously.
Question:
Due to the predominance of which primary element (*mahābhūta*) does the quality of smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) exist?
To speak at length, up to: "By the increase of which primary element (*mahābhūta*) does thirst arise?
Some say: "There is no [element] that increases exclusively."
However, regarding the distinctions among the categories of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are those capable of producing smoothness, and so on, up to those capable of producing thirst.

Furthermore, some say: because the water and fire elements increase, they produce smoothness; because the earth and wind elements increase, they produce roughness; because the fire and wind elements increase, they produce lightness; because the earth and water elements increase, they produce heaviness; because the water and wind elements increase, they produce cold; because only the wind element increases, it produces hunger; and because only the fire element increases, it produces thirst.

Regarding the statement "this increases," it means that its functional activity (*karmavṛtti*) increases, not its substantial entity (*dravya*). This is like the case of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
How is it so for the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)?
[The text continues] at length until: "that which falls under the category of form within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*)."
There are six kinds of falling:
first, falling into realms;
second, falling into destinies.
3. Falling into a person;
4. Falling into a location;
5. Falling into that which is with outflows.
Sixth, falling by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pāta*).
Regarding falling by way of realm (*dhātu-pāta*), it is as explained in the *Saṃyuktāgama* [or *Kṣudrakavastu*]:
"Whichever fetters (*saṃyojana*) fall into the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those fetters exist within the desire realm," and so forth.
"Fallen into a destiny" (*gati*) means that if one is included within such a destiny, one is said to have fallen into that destiny.
Regarding "a person who has fallen," as stated in the *Vinaya*:
"There are two types of persons who, having fallen into the number of the Saṃgha, cause the Saṃgha to be in harmony."
Regarding those included within the [sphere of] bases (*āyatana*), it is as explained herein.
What is non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
It refers to the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding those that "fall into the outflows" (*sāsrava*), it is as explained in this treatise.
What are the phenomena that fall? They are the phenomena associated with the outflows (*sāsravadharma*).
Regarding "falling into its own nature," it is as explained in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
What is the meaning of "appropriated" (*upātta*)?
Answer:

This unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa), which is a dharma included within its own substance as revealed by this designation, refers to the uninterrupted continuity of wholesome or unwholesome ethical discipline; it is at all times cognized by a single consciousness, namely the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), because it is non-resistant (apratigha).

The five objects, such as visible form and so forth, are cognized by the five consciousnesses in the present time, and by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) throughout the three periods of time.
These [objects] are cognized by the mental consciousness at all times; likewise, the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are also cognized by the mental consciousness at all times.
This non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is generally of two kinds: namely, wholesome and unwholesome.
There is no neutral (*avyākṛta*) kind, because a powerful mind can give rise to non-informative matter, whereas a neutral mind is weak and does not give rise to it.
All virtuous non-informative [forms] are generally of two kinds:
first, those subsumed under restraint; second, those not subsumed under restraint.
Non-virtuous non-informative [forms] are likewise of two kinds:
The first is that which is subsumed under non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and the second is that which is not subsumed under non-restraint.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) subsumed under restraint (*saṃvara*):

first, the restraint of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*); second, the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*); third, the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*); and fourth, the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
The prātimokṣa restraint refers to the precepts of the seven classes of followers.
The dhyāna restraint refers to the precepts of the form realm.
The untainted (anāsrava) restraint refers to the precepts of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

The restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*) is established based on one portion of two types of restraint, namely, the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*).

That which is subsumed under the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) for the purpose of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm is called the restraint of abandonment; it is so named because it can counteract all unwholesome conduct as well as the afflictions that give rise to unwholesome conduct.

The eight preceding paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that are included in the subsequent application (*anuvartaka*) are able to counteract only the afflictions that give rise to immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*).
The ninth path of immediate succession that is included in the subsequent application is able to counteract both immoral conduct and the afflictions that give rise to immoral conduct.
Question:
By what cause is the prātimokṣa restraint acquired, and by what cause is it relinquished?
Answer:
It is abandoned through four conditions due to the instruction of another.
What are these four?
First, the abandonment of the precepts one has undertaken;
2. Birth with both sexual organs;
3. Severing of the roots of goodness;
4. Loss of the homogeneous class.
Question:
By what cause is the dhyāna restraint obtained, and by what cause is it relinquished?
Answer:
The wholesome mind of the form realm is acquired when it is attained and abandoned when it is relinquished.
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, by way of falling away; [the second is by way of rebirth].
2. Because there is a transformation of realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
Question:
For what reason is the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) acquired, and for what reason is it relinquished?
Answer:
They are acquired simultaneously with the Path; there is no complete relinquishing of them.
If they are relinquished partially, it occurs by way of three conditions:
First, by way of falling away;
second, by way of attaining a fruit;
third, by way of transforming the faculties.
Question:
By what cause is the restraint of abandonment obtained, and by what cause is it relinquished?
Answer:
That which is comprised within the dhyāna restraint is as explained in the section on the dhyāna restraint.
That which is comprised within the untainted (anāsrava) restraint is as explained in the section on the untainted restraint.

Regarding the virtuous non-informative matter (avijñapti) subsumed under discipline (saṃvara): if a virtuous informative matter (vijñapti) is produced by a powerful pure mind, one obtains this non-informative matter;
if a virtuous informative matter is produced by an inferior pure mind, one does not obtain this non-informative matter.
This non-informative matter is relinquished through three conditions:
first, the cessation of the underlying intention;
second, the abandonment of the preparatory application; [and third, the death of the individual].
Third, the fault of limitation.

Regarding unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) subsumed under non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), this refers to the various forms of non-restraint, such as that of the sheep-slaughterers and so forth.
This non-restraint is acquired through two conditions:
First, by the performance of the action;
second, by the undertaking of the task.
This non-restraint is abandoned through four conditions:
First, by undertaking the prātimokṣa vows;
second, by attaining the dhyāna restraint;
third, by the arising of both sexual organs.
Fourth, [it ceases] by the loss of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, all matter (*rūpa*) is briefly of four kinds:
first, that which is maturation (*vipāka*);
Second, nurturance;
third, outflow;
fourth, momentariness.
Among these, the eye-base consists of only two types:

first, that which is maturation (*vipāka*); second, that which is nurtured (*aupacayika*). There is no separate type of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), because apart from the former two, there exists no distinct nature of outflow.
It should be understood that the same applies to the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As for the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it consists of only three types:
first, maturation (*vipāka*); second, nourishment (*aupacayika*); and third, outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
One should know that the same applies to the bases of odor, taste, and tangibility.
The base of sound has only two types; among the three previously mentioned, it excludes that which is maturation (*vipāka*).

The matter included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) also has only two types: that which is concomitant with the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is comprised of a single moment, while the remainder is comprised of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Chapter Two: The Examination of the Discerning Mind. Question:
It is already known that the characteristics of form deceive and delude the foolish; it cannot be grasped or touched, being like a mass of foam.
If one wishes to hear about the nature of the mind-dharmas, what are their characteristics?
Answer:
They are called mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna). One should not say "mind" alone, for that is precisely what is being asked.
Question:
What is the distinction between the three—citta, manas, and vijñāna?
Answer:
This lack of distinction is like worldly matters where one is spoken of as many, or many are spoken of as one.
An example of speaking of one as many is when a single person is called a "man," a "human being," a "youth," and so forth.

Regarding the frequent use of a single term: just as it is said that *māṣa* beans and the like are equally called "reborn" (*punarbhava*), one should know that here, too, the terms "mind" (*citta*), "mental faculty" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are likewise spoken of with reference to a single underlying entity.
Furthermore, there are those who say there is also a distinction:
that which is past is called *manas*, that which is future is called *citta*, and that which is present is called *vijñāna*.
Moreover, *citta* is designated in terms of the *dhātus*, *manas* in terms of the *āyatanas*, and *vijñāna* in terms of the *skandhas*.
Furthermore, it is called "mind" (*citta*) in the sense of karmic actions from a distant past; it is called "intellect" (*manas*) in the sense of karmic actions from the immediate past;

and it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the sense of karmic actions that project rebirth. Furthermore, it is called "mind" in the sense of accumulation; it is called "intellect" in the sense of orientation; and it is called "consciousness" in the sense of discernment.
Regarding the question, "What is meant by these six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*)?", it asks:
why are there exactly six, neither fewer nor more?
The answer is:

Because of [the requirements of] the bases and so forth; that is to say, the bases of consciousness are only six in number. If consciousness were reduced to five, then one base would be without consciousness; if consciousness were increased to seven, then one consciousness would be without a base. It should be understood that the same applies to the six objects of perception (*ālambana*).

However, when it is said that there are different consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), this refers to consciousness only in terms of its bases (*āśraya*). It is called a "body of consciousness" (*vijñānakāya*) because a single consciousness can have multiple [bases].
It is not that a single eye-consciousness is called an "eye-consciousness body"; rather, it is a plurality of eye-consciousnesses that is termed an "eye-consciousness body."
Just as a single elephant cannot be called an "elephant herd," but only when there are many elephants is it called an "elephant herd," so it is with this as well. What,
then, is eye-consciousness?
"Depending on the eye faculty" indicates the basis of visual consciousness;
"each discerning forms" indicates the object of visual consciousness.
Furthermore, "depending on the eye faculty" refers to the cause of visual consciousness, while "forms" refers to its condition.
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms.
Question:
What are the causes of the eye and visual consciousness?
Answer:
They are the supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*).
For example, it is like the primary elements (mahābhūta) acting as the basis and cause for derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
As for "each cognizing," this describes the characteristic of visual consciousness, because consciousness has cognition as its defining characteristic.
The meaning intended here is as follows: based on the eye and conditioned by visible forms, there arises the characteristic of discernment, which is called visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

This is explained in detail up to: based on the mind and conditioned by mental phenomena (*dharmas*), there arises the characteristic of discernment, which is called mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Question:
Why is it not simply stated that [consciousness] depends on the eye-faculty and so forth, or why is it not simply stated that each discerns form and so forth?
Answer:
If one were to state only one [of these factors], the meaning would not be established.

That is to say, if it were stated merely that [consciousness] depends on the eye-faculty and so forth, then the associated mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and others—which also depend on the eye-faculty and so forth—would likewise have to be called "eye-consciousness" and so forth.

If it were merely stated that each [consciousness] discerns form and so forth, then since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also discerns form and so forth, the mental consciousness would have to be designated as "eye-consciousness" and the rest.
However, by stating here that [the consciousnesses] depend on the eye-faculty and so forth, one excludes the mental consciousness which discerns form and so forth;
furthermore, by stating that each [of the six] discerns form and so forth, one excludes the feeling and other factors associated with the eye-consciousness and the rest.
Question:
Eye, visible form, light, and attention serve as conditions for the arising of visual consciousness; why then is it said that [visual consciousness] is [the eye-consciousness] and not the others?
Answer:
Because the eye-faculty is predominant;
because it is like dancing, dyeing, or writing; because the eye is not shared [with other faculties];

because it is the basis for the "eye-sprout" (cakṣur-aṅkura); because it is proximate to the eye, as in the case of the sound of a drum; and because it is taught as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses each have four types: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
The unwholesome type exists only in the desire realm.
The obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) exists only in the Brahma-world.

The wholesome and unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) are common to both the desire realm and the Brahma-world, but not to the higher stages, because [the higher stages] possess vitarka and vicāra.
The olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses each have three types, excluding the obscured-unspecified;
they exist only in the desire realm, as they take morsel food as their object.
Mental consciousness has four types, pervading the three realms and that which is unconditioned.
Question:
If the various stages above the first dhyāna lack the three bodies of consciousness (visual, auditory, and tactile), how can there be seeing, hearing, and touching for those born there?
Answer:
By the power of cultivation, the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna stage manifest, causing those three faculties to possess seeing, hearing, and touching.
Based on this principle, it is asked:
"Is it possible for a body of one stage, an eye of another stage, forms of another stage, and an eye-consciousness of another stage to arise?"
Answer: There is.
That is to say, one born in the stage of the second dhyāna uses the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage to see forms of the third dhyāna stage.

In this case, the body belongs to the second dhyāna level, the eye to the fourth dhyāna level, and the visible forms to the third dhyāna level; it is within this context that eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna level arises.
Each of the five groups of consciousness has two types:
first, that which is maturation (vipāka), and second, that which is outflowing (niṣyanda).
The group of mental consciousness has three types:
First is the ripened (vipāka), second is the outflowing (niṣyanda), and third is the momentary (kṣaṇika).
Among these, the "momentary" refers to the mental consciousness associated with the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
Question:

Is it possible that when a path consisting of a single cause manifests, the mind abandoned in a single moment may (1) have the nature of a homogeneous cause but lack a homogeneous cause; or (2) have a homogeneous cause but not have the nature of a homogeneous cause; or (3) have the nature of a homogeneous cause and also have a homogeneous cause; or (4) neither have the nature of a homogeneous cause nor have a homogeneous cause?
Answer:
At the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti), one should formulate four propositions.
The first proposition refers to the mind associated with the already-arisen patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti).
The second phrase refers to the mind associated with the future path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The third phrase refers to all other minds associated with the already-arisen path of seeing, excluding the mind associated with the already-arisen *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
Question:

Is it possible for a single path-factor to manifest, such that in a single moment the mind that is abandoned is either (1) with-outflows and has outflows as its object, (2) with-outflows and has outflows-free as its object, (3) outflows-free and has outflows-free as its object, or (4) outflows-free and has outflows as its object?
Answer: There are.
At the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti), one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first proposition refers to the mind associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which are connected to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) and have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*).

The second phrase refers to the mind associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga), which are bound to the realms of form and formlessness and take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
The third phrase refers to the mind associated with the receptivities (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) regarding cessation and the path.
The fourth phrase refers to the mind associated with the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Question:

Is there a case where the path that serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) to afflictions (*kleśa*) without an object (*avastuka*) manifests, and in a single moment, the mind that is abandoned is either (1) having an outflow (*sāsrava*) object while not having an outflow object as its focal condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or (2) having an outflow object while having an outflow object as its focal condition, or (3) not having an outflow object while not having an outflow object as its focal condition?
These four propositions should be contemplated according to their meaning.
Question:

Is there a momentary mind that manifests and thereby extinguishes a preceding mind which is either (1) neither fixed nor has a fixed object; or (2) neither fixed but has a fixed object; or (3) both fixed and has a fixed object; or (4) both fixed but does not have a fixed object?
These four propositions should be contemplated according to their meaning.
Question:

Is there a momentary mind that, upon manifesting, ceases a preceding mind, such that it has either (1) a mind already arisen as its cause, or (2) a mind not yet arisen as its cause, or (3) a mind already arisen as its cause while the other is not yet arisen, or (4) both a mind already arisen and a mind not yet arisen as its causes?
These four propositions should be contemplated according to their meaning.
Chapter Three: Analysis of Mental Factors (Caitasika-dharma-vibhāga) Question:

It has already been understood that [the mind] does not proceed from a single basis, object, or aspect, but flows like a magical illusion and is extremely difficult to subdue, like a wild elephant or horse, due to the various states of mind such as greed and so forth.
Now I wish to hear further regarding the characteristics of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
What are called mental factors?
How is it known that they exist separately [from the mind]?
Answer:
All that are called mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth,
exist as distinct entities, because the sūtras serve as the authoritative source for this knowledge.
As the Blessed One said:
"Eye-consciousness arises from the two conditions of the eye and visible forms; through the conjunction of these three, there is contact.
Arising together with contact, there are feeling, perception, and volition," and so forth, as extensively explained.
The *Satyavati-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, there is reflection upon the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), which arise dependent on the mind and are bound to the mind.
Moreover, Śāriputra asked Kauṇḍinya:
For what reason are perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*) called "mental formations" (*manosaṃskāra*)? Kautūhala said:
"These two mental factors arise depending on the mind and belong to the mind," and so forth, as explained at length.
Based on such immeasurable sūtras as these, it is known that mental factors (caitta-dharma) definitely possess a distinct substantial entity.

Furthermore, if mental factors lacked a distinct substantial entity, then the sūtras concerning śamatha, vipaśyanā, the roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla), the stations of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti), the nutriments (āhāra), the foundations of mindfulness (smṛty-upasthāna), the aggregates (skandha), the sixfold sets of factors of enlightenment (bodhy-aṅga) and the path (mārga-aṅga), the fetters (saṃyojana), the dharmas of training (śaikṣa-dharma), and the members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga) would have to be diminished.
Furthermore, one should not maintain that the "great ground dharmas" (mahābhūmika-dharma) and so forth do not exist;
for the dharma-gates taught in the sūtras are not deficient, and the great ground dharmas can indeed be established as real. Therefore, we know that there are distinct mental factors (caitta-dharma).
Question:
How can one know that mental factors are associated with the mind?
Answer:
Because the sūtras are authoritative, as the Blessed One said:
"Seeing is the root; faith is the realization associated with knowledge. Therefore, one knows that mental factors have the sense of being associated.
Question:
What is the meaning of "associated" (*saṃprayukta*)?
Answer:
The great masters of the Abhidharma all maintain this teaching:
that which is called "associated" (saṃprayukta) has the meaning of equality.
Question:

In some instances where the mind arises, mental factors (*caitta*) are numerous; in other instances where the mind arises, mental factors are few. How, then, can there be the sense of "equality" that constitutes the meaning of association (*samprayoga*)?
Answer:
This statement is made on the basis of equality regarding their substance (*dravya*).
If within a single moment of mind there were two feelings and one perception, they could not be equal; this would be the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*).

However, within a single moment of mind there is only one feeling and one perception, and the same applies to volition (*cetanā*) and the other mental factors; therefore, it is said that equality is the meaning of association.
Furthermore, being equal and non-contradictory is the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*).
Being equal and not dispersed is the meaning of association.
Operating in equality is the meaning of association.
Just as a chariot is so named because of its various parts, it is called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) for this reason.
Furthermore, the meaning of association is that they share the same time, the same basis, the same aspect, the same object, the same result, the same outflow, and the same maturation.
What, then, is this? It refers to feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), and so forth, as explained at length.
Question:
Why is feeling (vedanā) taught first, rather than perception (saṃjñā) and the others?
Answer:
Because its mode of activity (ākāra) is coarse.
Although feeling (*vedanā*) is unimpeded and does not abide in a specific location, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse, as it is designated (*prajñapti*) in the same manner as form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, worldly people say:
"I now have pain in my hand, pain in my foot, pain in my head," and so forth, as explained at length.
Perception, volition, contact, and so forth do not possess such a nature.
What is feeling? It is defined as the quality of experiencing.
That which possesses the function of experiencing is called the nature of experience (*anubhava-svabhāva*), which means the sense of receiving an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

This is of three kinds: pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*). Among these, that which can nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) through an even state of reception is termed pleasant feeling.
If one can diminish the nature of sensation arising from the inequality of the sense faculties and the primary elements, it is called a painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
Contrary to these two, a nature of sensation that is neither equal nor unequal is called a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

Furthermore, if within this feeling the latent tendency of greed increases by way of two conditions—namely, by way of the object of perception (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*)—this is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

If, regarding this feeling, the latent tendency of aversion increases through two conditions—namely, by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*)—it is called a painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*).

If, regarding this feeling, the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) increases through two conditions—namely, by way of the object or by way of association—it is called a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

Although the latent tendency of delusion increases in two ways in relation to all feelings, it does not arise in dependence on delusion nor does it proceed by its own power; rather, it most frequently coexists with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The others are not mentioned because they are clearly understood.

Since there are distinctions among objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, and conducive to equanimity, these three modes of experience (*anubhava*) are established; therefore, it is said that there are only three types of feeling (*vedanā*), yet in reality, the nature of feeling is of immeasurable kinds.
There are others who maintain that there is no truly real pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) nor neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).
Question:
For what reason do they say that there is no truly real pleasant feeling?
Answer:
Because the sūtras are the authoritative source.
As it is stated in the sūtra:
There is no sensation whatsoever that is not suffering.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"You should contemplate pleasant sensations as suffering."
If the nature of pleasant feeling were substantially existent, how could the Blessed One instruct his disciples to contemplate pleasure as suffering?
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"To regard suffering as pleasure is called a perversion."

If there were such a thing as pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), there would be no suffering; that is to say, there would be no perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"All contaminated feelings (*sāsrava-vedanā*) are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)."
Regarding what is included herein, it is inclusion by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since pleasant feeling is not real, its intrinsic nature is suffering.
How, then, can it be said to be included within the Truth of Suffering?
Since it has already been stated that [feeling] is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there is no such thing as a truly real pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

Furthermore, because their characteristics differ—namely, that which has the characteristic of oppression is called "suffering"—a truly real pleasant feeling cannot possess the characteristic of oppression. How, then, can it be said that all contaminated feelings (*sāsrava-vedanā*) are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering?
Furthermore, it is because of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). That is to say, observing that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are suffering is termed "clear realization.

If the nature of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) were substantially real, then observing pleasure as suffering would constitute a perverted view (*viparyāsa-dṛṣṭi*) and could not be considered clear realization. Therefore, one must certainly know that there is no substantially real pleasant feeling.
The Abhidharma masters say:
"Pleasurable sensation (sukha-vedanā) truly exists, because the Sūtra is the authoritative source (pramāṇa).
That is to say, the Sūtra states:"
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"If form were exclusively suffering and not pleasure, and were not accompanied by pleasure, sentient beings would not become attached to forms.
This is explained at length.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Together with pleasure and together with joy, I speak of the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths.
Another sutra says:
There are three kinds of feeling (vedanā): pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"When pleasant feelings arise and when they persist, they are pleasant; yet they have the affliction of impermanence."
When various painful feelings arise and while they endure, suffering exists because of the fault of impermanence.

If the nature of pleasant feeling were not truly existent, it should not be spoken of as being of the same category as suffering; rather, it should be spoken of as a distinct category from pleasant feeling, and it should be spoken of as a distinct category from painful feeling.
Furthermore, if pleasant feeling were not substantially existent, there would be no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), as it would lack a cause.
As the Sūtra says:
"Because of joy (*prīti*), there is pliancy of body and mind."

If there were no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), there would likewise be no bliss; this would extend even further until there were no nirvana at all, because there would be no gradual causes, as the effects would not exist.
Regarding this, that teacher offers a defense, saying:
"Just as in the higher stages there is no joy (*prīti*), yet there is no absence of physical and mental pliancy; therefore, the cited proof is not definitive. That defense is irrational.
Why is this? Because there is no joy whatsoever in the higher stages.
One should contemplate this meaning as it is explained in the *Gandharva-sūtra* regarding the conjunction of the three factors and the nutriment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:

"When parents are in union, a *gandharva* appears before them; yet there are times when, even without the union of parents, a *gandharva* likewise appears—such as those who undergo moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*) or transformation-birth (*upapāduka*). For sentient beings born from a womb or an egg, there is no possibility of entering the womb apart from the conjunction of parents."
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"The conjunction of three things is called life-span (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

However, although there is no warmth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is life-span and consciousness; yet in the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), life-span and consciousness do not exist apart from warmth.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"The body subsists by depending on nutriment; this is not the case for the two higher realms.
Abiding is due to the three nutriments, and the same applies to the desire realm."
It is not that those dwelling in the desire realm subsist by means of the four nutriments; the same applies to the higher realms.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:

"Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness, and consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form. Although there is no form in the formless realm, name and consciousness still condition one another in turn, thereby establishing this same principle for the desire and form realms as well.
It is the same here: if there is a basis for joy (*prīti*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) arises because of that joy;
however, if joy is absent in a certain state, pliancy may still be present due to other conditions, so one should not raise an objection.
What are the remaining conditions?
They are as follows: first, the superior feeling of joy in the desire realm induces the pliancy of the *anāgamya* concentration to arise;
second, the superior feeling of joy in the first and second dhyānas induces the pliancy of the higher stages to arise.
If there were no joy at all, there would be no pliancy; from this it is proven that there must be the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).

Furthermore, it is like the case of those in the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) who, though unable to attain [certain higher states] while in the two upper realms, are nonetheless able to attain the fruit of Arhatship because they are drawn by the power of their prior [attainments].
This case should be understood in the same way; one should not find fault with it.
Furthermore, it is like a wheel that continues to spin even after a staff has been removed once it has first been struck by the staff.

This should be understood similarly: the power of prior joy (*prīti*) induces subsequent pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Therefore, pliancy necessarily depends upon joy. Since joy is comprised within the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*), it is known for certain that the feeling of pleasure truly exists.
Furthermore, because pleasant feeling involves aspiration, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"If one possesses pleasure, there is aspiration for phenomena.
If pleasant feeling did not exist, there would be no aspiration for phenomena; therefore, one must certainly know that pleasant feeling truly exists.
Furthermore, agreeable karma would be without fruit; if there were no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), all agreeable karma would be empty and fruitless.

Since all agreeable karma necessarily has pleasant feeling as its fruit, one should not say that agreeable karma has the requisites of pleasure (*sukha-sādhana*) as its ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), because the requisites of pleasure are merely dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*). That is to say, the requisites of pleasure are dominant fruits, not ripened fruits.
Why is this so? Because all articles of pleasure can be enjoyed in common with others, and because they are not lost or destroyed after one's own death.

That is to say, while various articles of pleasure may be enjoyed in common with other sentient beings, the fruits of karmic maturation (*vipāka-phala*) certainly have no sense of being shared in common with others; for they fall within one's own continuum and are not common to others.
Furthermore, after one's life has ended, the various instruments of pleasure—such as elephants, horses, and so forth—remain without being lost or destroyed.

Since the various results of maturation (*vipāka*) coexist with the body and life, they would certainly be lost and destroyed if the body and life were absent; therefore, it is logically certain that if there were no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), desirable karma would be empty and fruitless.

Furthermore, because there is nourishment and benefit: if there were no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would lack such nourishment and benefit.
If it is argued that nourishment and benefit arise from sentient beings' conceptualization of objects rather than from pleasant feeling, this reasoning is also incorrect.
One should understand that there is benefit through inclusion, just as there is harm due to painful sensation.
Furthermore, because correct application must necessarily have a result, if pleasant sensation did not exist, then correct application would be empty and fruitless.
Regarding right application, it should have painful sensation as its ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), because there is no pleasant sensation;

for just as wrong application must necessarily have painful sensation as its ripening fruit, right application should have pleasant sensation as its ripening fruit, as they are mutually contradictory, like light and darkness, or shadow and light.
Furthermore, because unwholesome conduct arises from pleasant feeling, if pleasant feeling did not exist, unwholesome conduct would likewise not exist.
It is because sentient beings are attached to pleasant feeling that they engage in various unwholesome acts, which result in the fruit of painful feeling.

If unwholesome conduct did not exist, there would be no painful feeling; since painful feeling exists, unwholesome conduct is not non-existent. Since unwholesome conduct exists, pleasant feeling must certainly exist. Furthermore, because it is a dharma that is experienced (*vedanīya*), as stated in the Sūtra:

"There are four types of dharmas that are experienced: some dharmas that are experienced as pleasant in the present and painful in the future; some dharmas that are experienced as painful in the present and pleasant in the future; some dharmas that are experienced as pleasant in the present and pleasant in the future; and some dharmas that are experienced as painful in the present and painful in the future."
If there were no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), then mental feeling (*dharma-vedanā*) would be of only one kind;
it should not be fourfold. For such various reasons as these, pleasant feeling definitely exists.
Question:
If there is a feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), what is the underlying principle behind the Blessed One’s statement in the *Sūtra on Contradiction with the Feeling of Pleasure*?
Answer:
There is a distinct underlying principle.

Furthermore, regarding the initial sutra statement that "all sensations whatsoever are none other than suffering," one should know that this sutra speaks in reliance upon the three types of suffering.
What are these three sufferings? First is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Second is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).

If all painful sensations (*duḥkhavedanā*) are called "suffering" by virtue of the suffering of suffering, if all pleasant sensations (*sukhavedanā*) are called "suffering" by virtue of the suffering of change, and if all neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*) are called "suffering" by virtue of the suffering of conditioned formations, then one should understand that the Sūtra’s statement that "because they are impermanent, they are suffering" follows this underlying principle.
